title: A2 DRAFT: Spark and Glue: Exploring performance and cost
text:
WarningDraft, watch for updates



This is a draft of Assignment 2. The commands, the code and some details may still change before the release, and the released version is the one that counts. The commands now sit inside the assignment, in the collapsed 📋 blocks, and there is no separate job aid page.

title: A2 DRAFT: Spark and Glue: Exploring performance and cost
text:
The code you run
Everything you run is in the starter repository. Each file opens on GitHub, so you can read it before you run it:

stages/stage1_duckdb.py: runs Stage 1, DuckDB reading the trip files from S3 and writing the model matrix
stages/stage2_spark.py: the one Spark job behind Stages 2a, 2b and 3, on EMR and on Glue
stages/parse_run_log.py: turns a run’s metrics blocks into results.csv rows
results.csv: the header you fill in, one row per stage and phase

The scripts above also time themselves and print metrics, which makes the work hard to see. Two shorter files hold only the work, the same queries and computation with the timing left out. They are for reading; the graded runs use the scripts above.

workload/stage1.sql: the query Stage 1 runs
workload/stage2.py: the Spark work of Stages 2a, 2b and 3, from the join to the 60 fits

title: A2 DRAFT: Spark and Glue: Exploring performance and cost
text:
Your shells and variables
Everything in this assignment runs in the AWS console, in your browser. There is no AWS command to run on your laptop, which only keeps results.csv and your screenshots. Two shells do the work:

CloudShell, a terminal inside the AWS console (the >_ icon in the top bar). It already has the AWS CLI and your credentials, and it runs every command except the Stage 1 job itself.
Session Manager on the Stage 1 instance, which you open from the EC2 console. It runs the Stage 1 job.




Commands
Shell
What has to stay running




Once per account, Get the data
CloudShell
the tab, until the fetch loop finishes. CloudShell’s home directory survives closing it


run-instances in Stage 1 on one EC2 instance
CloudShell
nothing


the Stage 1 run itself, and its parse
Session Manager on the Stage 1 instance
the tab, for the length of the run. Anything written to that disk dies when you terminate the instance


creating the cluster in Launch the cluster
the EMR console, in your browser
nothing. Its AWS CLI export goes into launch-cluster.sh in CloudShell


the rest of Launch the cluster through Stage 3 on Glue, and Shut down and verify
CloudShell
nothing in the shell. The cluster and the Glue job run on AWS whether the tab is open or not


results.csv and the three screenshots
your laptop
they stay on your laptop from the first row you write to the moment you submit



The commands name your resources through shell variables such as $BUCKET, so you can paste them unchanged. You set the variables once, in CloudShell. They live in ~/a2.env, a file in CloudShell’s home folder that survives closing the tab, and a line in ~/.bashrc loads it into every new CloudShell tab. In CloudShell, put your CWL in place of yourcwl, in lowercase, and run:
cat > ~/a2.env <<'EOF'
export CWL=yourcwl
export BUCKET=436c-a2-$CWL
save() { export "$1=$2"; echo "export $1=$2" >> ~/a2.env; echo "$1=$2"; }
EOF
grep -qs a2.env ~/.bashrc || echo 'source ~/a2.env' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/a2.env
echo $BUCKET
The last line prints 436c-a2- and your CWL. Every other variable is an id AWS hands you along the way: the subnet, the instance, the cluster, each step, the Glue run. The command that creates each id saves it with save, which adds a line to ~/a2.env, so you do not type ids by hand. The one exception is the cluster id, which you copy from the EMR console. cat ~/a2.env shows everything saved so far.
CloudShell also needs uv, the Python tool the data step uses, once:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

title: A2 DRAFT: Spark and Glue: Exploring performance and cost
text:
Roles
Three things happen once per account, before anything else: EMR gets the service roles it will not launch without, your bucket gets created, and the Stage 1 instance gets a role of its own. They are one block of commands, and it is the first block you run (see 📋 below). A1’s role does not carry over, because it is scoped to the a1 bucket.







Note📋 Commands: Once per account





All of this runs in CloudShell. EMR will not launch without its service roles.
aws emr create-default-roles --region ca-central-1
A reply saying the roles already exist is a success. Then make the bucket, in the same region.
aws s3 mb s3://$BUCKET --region ca-central-1
Course accounts have no default network (VPC), so every launch names a subnet. Find the account’s public subnet and save it.
SUBNET=$(aws ec2 describe-subnets --region ca-central-1 \
  --filters Name=map-public-ip-on-launch,Values=true \
  --query 'Subnets[0].SubnetId' --output text)
save SUBNET "$SUBNET"
It prints SUBNET=subnet-..., and every launch in this assignment uses that subnet. If it prints SUBNET=None, post on Piazza with your account id and the exact output. Meanwhile you can do everything up to the launch step: the data fetch and the predictions need no instance.
A2’s Stage 1 instance needs its own role, and A1’s will not do: A1’s is scoped to the a1 bucket and carries no Session Manager permission. Build the new one the way A1 built its role, create first and permissions after, then wrap it in an instance profile, which is the object EC2 actually accepts.
cat > ~/a2-s3-policy.json <<EOF
{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":["s3:GetObject","s3:PutObject","s3:DeleteObject","s3:ListBucket"],"Resource":["arn:aws:s3:::$BUCKET","arn:aws:s3:::$BUCKET/*"]}]}
EOF
aws iam create-role --role-name $CWL-a2-role \
  --assume-role-policy-document '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"ec2.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole"}]}'
aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name $CWL-a2-role \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore
aws iam put-role-policy --role-name $CWL-a2-role --policy-name a2-s3 \
  --policy-document file://$HOME/a2-s3-policy.json
aws iam create-instance-profile --instance-profile-name $CWL-a2-role
aws iam add-role-to-instance-profile --instance-profile-name $CWL-a2-role --role-name $CWL-a2-role
AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore is what lets you open a shell on the instance with no key pair and no inbound rule. The inline policy is your bucket, and only your bucket. IAM takes about ten seconds to propagate, so a run-instances fired immediately after the last line can come back saying the instance profile does not exist. Wait, then run it again.









Tip💡 Why a role and not a login



A general (simplified!) rule: instances and services get roles, people get accounts with logins. If you need to assign some permissions to an EC2 instance, an EMR cluster or Glue, you need to create a role allowing them to do something on your behalf. Remember that in A1 we created instance and execution roles; here in A2 we use the default EMR service roles and create a Glue role following the 📋 commands in Stage 3, and in Stage 3 you will create one custom yourself. Every time you see an “access denied” type of error, you need to check for a missing role, or a permission you need to add.

title: A2 DRAFT: Spark and Glue: Exploring performance and cost
text:
Bucket and data
Create s3://436c-a2-<your CWL>/ and put 40 objects in it: the 39 monthly trip files from the New York Taxi and Limousine Commission (TLC) distribution, and the zone lookup, which arrives as CSV and is converted to Parquet once as zones.parquet. The fetch loop runs for a few minutes, so start it before you read the rest of this (see 📋 below). The files travel from the TLC’s public file service into your bucket, so nothing here is downloaded to your laptop.







Note📋 Commands: Get the data





Thirty-nine monthly yellow-taxi files, January 2022 to March 2025, and the zone lookup, straight from the New York Taxi and Limousine Commission (TLC) distribution into your bucket. Run this in CloudShell, before the Stage 1 instance exists. It moves about 2 GB and takes a few minutes, so start it before you read ahead. Each file is deleted after it lands in S3, which keeps the local disk from filling.
for Y in 2022 2023 2024; do
  for M in 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 10 11 12; do
    curl -sSfO "https://d37ci6vzurychx.cloudfront.net/trip-data/yellow_tripdata_${Y}-${M}.parquet"
    aws s3 cp "yellow_tripdata_${Y}-${M}.parquet" s3://$BUCKET/a2/raw/ --region ca-central-1
    rm "yellow_tripdata_${Y}-${M}.parquet"
  done
done

for M in 2025-01 2025-02 2025-03; do
  curl -sSfO "https://d37ci6vzurychx.cloudfront.net/trip-data/yellow_tripdata_${M}.parquet"
  aws s3 cp "yellow_tripdata_${M}.parquet" s3://$BUCKET/a2/raw/ --region ca-central-1
  rm "yellow_tripdata_${M}.parquet"
done
The lookup ships as CSV. The Stage 2a job reads it as Parquet, with the columns LocationID, Borough, and Zone, so convert it once before you need it.
curl -sSfO "https://d37ci6vzurychx.cloudfront.net/misc/taxi_zone_lookup.csv"
uv run --with duckdb python3 -c "
import duckdb
duckdb.sql('''COPY (SELECT LocationID, Borough, Zone
                    FROM read_csv_auto('taxi_zone_lookup.csv'))
              TO 'zones.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET)''')
"
aws s3 cp zones.parquet s3://$BUCKET/a2/raw/zones.parquet --region ca-central-1
Check what landed before you launch anything. You want 40 objects: 39 trip files and zones.parquet. A short count means a curl failed partway through the loop, so re-run it: the files already in the bucket are simply overwritten.
aws s3 ls s3://$BUCKET/a2/raw/ --summarize --human-readable --region ca-central-1
Prediction 1 starts from the size of the trip files, so total those 39 on their own. The lookup is not part of what Stage 1 reads.
aws s3 ls s3://$BUCKET/a2/raw/yellow_tripdata_ --summarize --human-readable --region ca-central-1

title: A2 DRAFT: Spark and Glue: Exploring performance and cost
text:
The results file
results.csv ships with the assignment, header only. Keep it on your laptop, from the first row you write to the moment you submit, and append one row per stage-phase there: seven rows in all, one for Stage 1, two each for Stages 2a and 2b, two for Stage 3. Nothing you run in the cloud writes to this file. The Stage 1 instance is terminated before you hand anything in, so a copy that lives only on it is a copy you lose.
Four of its columns need explaining. resource_id is the instance, cluster, or Glue job-run ID, and it has to match a screenshot. predicted_s is your prediction, entered before the run. wall_s and startup_s stay in separate columns. cost_usd comes from AWS’s price pages for EC2 on-demand instances, EMR and Glue, read for ca-central-1, not from the billing console.
The order of work within a row is fixed. Write that row’s predicted_s from the prediction block first, before you launch anything. Then run the stage, tee its output to a log file, and hand the log to stages/parse_run_log.py, which prints the measured row to the shell with predicted_s empty by design. Copy the measured values into the row you already wrote, or paste the printed row in and type your prediction back into it. The parser never produces predicted_s. That number is yours, and the notebook cell you wrote it in is what dates it.
Before you parse a log, glance at Did the run work? below: four lines that tell you whether the run is worth reading at all.







Note📋 Did the run work?





Four lines to glance at in a log before you parse it. If any of them is wrong, the run is not comparable to your others, and re-running is the only fix.

The block arrived. grep -c '===A2-METRICS' YOUR.log prints 1 for Stage 1 and 2 for Stages 2a, 2b and 3. A 0 means the script stopped early, and the reason sits above where the block should have been. The first check applies to every run. The other three apply to the Spark runs only: Stage 1’s block reads mode=duckdb and has no retry or shuffle keys.
mode=rest in every Stage 2 and Stage 3 block, with rest_target naming the host the metrics reader reached. A cluster or Glue run that exits 3 reached no Spark REST endpoint and measured nothing. That is a failed run, not a slow one.
retried=0. A 1 means a stage or task was retried, so the timings are not comparable: rerun.
shuffle_partitions reads 16, and partitions in the phase A block reads the same 16. If the two disagree, the shuffle setting did not take and your two node counts stop being comparable. The one run where both read 8 instead is the optional extension below, and it is the only one. tasks is a different number and is meant to move with the cluster.

title: A2 DRAFT: Spark and Glue: Exploring performance and cost
text:
1.1 Predict
rubric={reasoning:5}






Tip📐 Prediction 1, how long will Stage 1 take?



predicted_seconds ≈ bytes_to_read / read_rate

Bytes to read. In CloudShell, total the size of the 39 trip files:
aws s3 ls s3://$BUCKET/a2/raw/yellow_tripdata_ --summarize --human-readable --region ca-central-1
The script reads 6 of the 19 columns in each file. The 2025 files have one extra column, which you don’t need. Based on this, estimate how many bytes you expect to read, and pay for. Give a one- or two-sentence explanation.
Read rate. The instance page lists the m7g.xlarge network as “up to 12.5 Gb/s”. Write the rate you will actually use in your prediction, in bytes per second, and where it came from.

All data has to come through the network before DuckDB can read it, so the network is one candidate limit (L2’s throughput table). Compare the rate you achieve with it, and say what else could be the limit (L4: the CPU that decompresses and parses).
Write your prediction into the predicted_s cell of your Stage 1 row before you run the stage. The script prints the measured time, so run it only after your prediction is written.


The parser will key that row stage=1_duckdb, phase=scan.

title: A2 DRAFT: Spark and Glue: Exploring performance and cost
text:
1.2 Measure
rubric={correctness:5}
Launch one m7g.xlarge with your CWL in the name from CloudShell, then run the script from a shell on the instance itself (see 📋 below). It prints one metrics block.







Note📋 Commands: Stage 1 on one EC2 instance





From CloudShell, launch one m7g.xlarge on Amazon Linux 2023 with the instance profile you made under Once per account.
INSTANCE_ID=$(aws ec2 run-instances --region ca-central-1 \
  --image-id resolve:ssm:/aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-arm64 \
  --instance-type m7g.xlarge \
  --count 1 \
  --subnet-id $SUBNET \
  --iam-instance-profile Name=$CWL-a2-role \
  --block-device-mappings 'DeviceName=/dev/xvda,Ebs={VolumeSize=60,VolumeType=gp3}' \
  --tag-specifications "ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=a2-stage1-$CWL}]" \
  --query 'Instances[0].InstanceId' --output text)
save INSTANCE_ID "$INSTANCE_ID"
The root volume is sized at 60 GiB because the AL2023 default of 8 GiB leaves little room once the Python toolchain and its packages are installed. The raw files never touch this disk: DuckDB reads them from S3 and writes its result back there. /dev/xvda is AL2023’s root device name. The image name ends in arm64 because an m7g.xlarge is a Graviton (ARM) instance, and an x86_64 image does not boot on it. If you launch from the console instead, pick the 64-bit (Arm) architecture for the same reason.
Connect from the EC2 console: select the instance, choose Connect, then the Session Manager tab. There is no key pair and no inbound SSH rule anywhere in this assignment. The session opens in /usr/bin, a folder you cannot write to, so the first line below moves to your home folder. Then clone the repo and work from its root, because stages/stage1_duckdb.py imports a helper out of stages/stage2_spark.py and a single copied file will not run.
In CloudShell, run cat ~/a2.env and copy the lines that start with export. Paste them into the Session Manager shell, so $BUCKET and $INSTANCE_ID mean the same thing there.
cd ~
sudo dnf install -y git
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
git clone https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/a2-starter.git && cd a2-starter
Now run the stage and keep the output.
uv run --python 3.11 \
  --with duckdb --with pyspark --with numpy --with "pandas<3" --with pyyaml \
  python3 stages/stage1_duckdb.py \
    --trips "s3://$BUCKET/a2/raw/yellow_tripdata_*.parquet" \
    --out s3://$BUCKET/a2/matrix.parquet \
    --window-start 2022-01-01 --window-end 2025-04-01 \
  | tee stage1.log
The --trips glob is quoted so DuckDB expands the *, not your shell. --python 3.11 overrides the system Python, which on Amazon Linux 2023 is 3.9. pyspark, numpy, and pandas are there for one import at the top of the script and run none of the query.
If the run stops on a Secret Validation Failure before it prints anything, the instance has no credentials to sign the S3 reads with: the instance profile is missing from the instance, so attach <your CWL>-a2-role to the instance and run it again.
Turn the log into a results.csv row. Confirm the metrics block arrived first: grep -c '===A2-METRICS' stage1.log prints 1.
python3 stages/parse_run_log.py stage1.log --resource-id $INSTANCE_ID --nodes 1
It prints the row to the shell and writes nothing. Copy what it prints into the results.csv on your laptop, next to the prediction you put in that row before the run: the parser leaves predicted_s empty every time, and your own copy of the file is the only place that number exists.
Leave the instance running if you want it for the S3 listings in Stage 2a’s prediction blocks. It is the cheapest thing in the assignment, and Shut down and verify is where it dies.










Key
What it is




wall_s
the run’s duration, and what the parser puts in your Stage 1 row


bytes_on_disk
compressed size of every column in the files it opened


bytes_needed
compressed size of the 6 columns it read


rows_in, rows_out
rows before the filter, rows after


mb_per_s_per_core
the per-core read rate the run achieved. Stage 2a predicts from this



Parse the log into your Stage 1 row and fill in cost_usd from the EC2 rate for ca-central-1.






Tip📸 Screenshot 1



The instance page while it runs: instance ID, type, launch time, CWL in the name. The instance ID must equal resource_id in your Stage 1 row.








Tip👀 Quick check




bytes_needed should be well below bytes_on_disk but not tiny: the columns are of different size. If it comes back at zero, or equal to bytes_on_disk, the run did not work: run it again.
The rate you achieved should land well below the advertised 12.5 Gb/s. If yours lands above it, check your units: the metrics key is megabytes per second, the instance page gigabits per second.
The timed pass, wall_s, should take well under a minute.







NoteCompare with our run, open after you have written your explanation





In our runs almost all of Stage 1’s wall time was the read. The filter and the write cost very little next to it.

title: A2 DRAFT: Spark and Glue: Exploring performance and cost
text:
1.3 Explain the gap
rubric={reasoning:10}

Set your Stage 1 prediction against your measured wall_s. About right, out by a factor of a few, or out by an order of magnitude? Say which term was wrong and in which direction.
You paid for fewer bytes than the files hold. Name what in the file format let the reader skip the rest, and say why the saving stops where it does.
The instance page advertises 12.5 Gb/s and you did not get it. What is that figure measuring, and why is it the wrong number to predict a sustained read with?
You could have run this stage on 3 instances instead of 1, at roughly 3 times the hourly rate. What would that have bought here, and what would the work need to look like for extra instances to help?

title: A2 DRAFT: Spark and Glue: Exploring performance and cost
text:
2a.1 Predict
rubric={reasoning:4}






Tip📐 Prediction 2, how long will phase A take?



time_A ≈ rows / (cores × rows_per_second_per_core)

Rows. rows_out from your Stage 1 metrics block, which is what matrix.parquet holds. Write the number down.
Rows per second per core. Stage 1’s rows_out divided by its wall_s, divided again by its 4 cores. That rate prices a scan and phase A also aggregates, so write the rate you are using and say that it makes your answer a floor.
Cores. Core nodes times the 4 vCPU an m7g.xlarge has. No task runs on the primary node (L5), so count only core-node cores. Write the core count you are predicting with.

Phase A has 16 partitions to hand out and a partition is worked on by one core, so 8 cores work through them in two waves and 16 cores in one. Say what that does to the formula above at each node count.








Tip📐 Prediction 3, how long will phase B take?



time_B ≈ ceil(fits / cores) × seconds_per_fit

Fits. 60, from 12 combinations on 5 folds. The job prints it back as fits_done. Write it into the formula.
Seconds per fit. You have measured no fit yet, so write a defensible estimate with one sentence of reasoning. After the 2-node run you replace it with a measured figure.
Cores. The same core count as in prediction 2.

Phase B has 60 independent fits and no shuffle. Each core runs one fit at a time, so the fits go in waves of as many fits as you have cores. ceil rounds up because a last, partly full wave still takes a whole fit’s time (L6).


Both predictions go into results.csv before you submit the step.

title: A2 DRAFT: Spark and Glue: Exploring performance and cost
text:
2a.2 Measure
rubric={correctness:4}






Warning⚠️ Finish Setup’s bucket and data, and Stage 1, before you start the cluster



The cluster writes its logs to s3://436c-a2-<your CWL>/a2/emr-logs/, and every step reads matrix.parquet, which Stage 1 writes to the same bucket. The bucket and its data come from Bucket and data in Setup. Check both before you choose Create cluster: aws s3 ls s3://436c-a2-<your CWL>/a2/ should list raw/ and matrix.parquet. A cluster started without them bills from the moment it launches and can do nothing useful, and a step submitted without matrix.parquet fails with The given path is invalid.


Build the cluster in the EMR console: 1 primary and 2 core m7g.xlarge, release emr-spark-8.0.0, Spark, the idle termination setting left on, and your CWL in the cluster name. Before you leave the cluster page, export its definition as a CLI command and save it as launch-cluster.sh. If the cluster terminates, that command rebuilds it exactly. The settings, the export, and the fallback are in the 📋 block below. Every command from here to the end of the assignment runs in CloudShell.







Note📋 Console steps and commands: Launch the cluster





First check that the bucket holds the data and Stage 1’s output, because the cluster logs to it and every step reads from it. The bucket comes from Once per account, the data from Get the data, and matrix.parquet from Stage 1 on one EC2 instance.
aws s3 ls s3://$BUCKET/a2/        # expect raw/ and matrix.parquet
In the EMR console (EMR on EC2 → Clusters → Create cluster), set these and leave everything else at its default:

Name and applications: cluster name a2- followed by your CWL; Amazon EMR release emr-spark-8.0.0, picked exactly, since the console offers later 8.0.x releases and those are different builds; application bundle Spark
Cluster configuration: instance groups, with Primary 1 × m7g.xlarge and Core 2 × m7g.xlarge; remove the Task group if the wizard offers one
Networking: your subnet, which echo $SUBNET prints in CloudShell
Cluster termination: keep automatic termination after idle time on, and set it to 15 minutes. It is the difference between a $2 assignment and a $60 one if you close your laptop at the wrong moment
Cluster logs: the path echo s3://$BUCKET/a2/emr-logs/ prints in CloudShell
IAM roles: service role EMR_DefaultRole, instance profile EMR_EC2_DefaultRole, the two that create-default-roles made

Choose Create cluster. On the cluster’s page, choose AWS CLI export and paste the command it shows into a new file in CloudShell, launch-cluster.sh. It reads like this, with your own subnet and bucket where this shows $SUBNET and $BUCKET:
aws emr create-cluster --region ca-central-1 \
  --name "a2-$CWL" \
  --release-label emr-spark-8.0.0 \
  --applications Name=Spark \
  --ec2-attributes SubnetId=$SUBNET \
  --instance-groups \
      InstanceGroupType=MASTER,InstanceCount=1,InstanceType=m7g.xlarge \
      InstanceGroupType=CORE,InstanceCount=2,InstanceType=m7g.xlarge \
  --use-default-roles \
  --auto-termination-policy IdleTimeout=900 \
  --log-uri s3://$BUCKET/a2/emr-logs/
Check three things in the copy: the release label, InstanceCount=2 on the CORE group, and IdleTimeout=900. If the cluster terminates before you are done, run bash launch-cluster.sh in CloudShell or repeat the console steps. Either builds the same cluster again.
The cluster id, j-..., is on the cluster page. It is the one id you copy by hand: put yours in place of the j- value below.
save CLUSTER_ID j-XXXXXXXXXXXXX
Then poll until the state reads WAITING. The same call returns the launch’s start and end, so you do not time it yourself.
aws emr describe-cluster --cluster-id $CLUSTER_ID --region ca-central-1 \
  --query 'Cluster.Status.{State:State,Created:Timeline.CreationDateTime,Ready:Timeline.ReadyDateTime}'
launch_s is Ready minus Created, in seconds. The EMR console shows the same two stamps under the cluster’s timeline if you would rather read them there. Save it, with your number in place of 412:
save LAUNCH_S 412



Time the launch: the gap from the create call to the cluster reaching WAITING is launch_s, which prediction 4 needs later. You pay that wait once and then run twice. Now submit the job as a step (see 📋 below). It prints one metrics block per phase.







Note📋 Commands: Submit the job as a step





CloudShell needs its own copy of the starter repo: the clone you made in Stage 1 lived on the instance. Clone it here once, then upload the job script. Every later run reads this same object, on both platforms.
cd ~
[ -d a2-starter ] || git clone https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/a2-starter.git
cd ~/a2-starter
aws s3 cp stages/stage2_spark.py s3://$BUCKET/a2/stages/stage2_spark.py --region ca-central-1
Submit it as a step. --deploy-mode client keeps the driver on the primary node, which is what puts its stdout in the step’s own log. The step passes no partition argument, so the job runs at its own default of 16 shuffle partitions and prints that back as shuffle_partitions in every metrics block. Both graded runs use the default, and so does Stage 3.
STEP_ID=$(aws emr add-steps --cluster-id $CLUSTER_ID --region ca-central-1 \
  --steps "Type=Spark,Name=a2-stage2-2n,ActionOnFailure=CONTINUE,Args=[--deploy-mode,client,s3://$BUCKET/a2/stages/stage2_spark.py,--trips,s3://$BUCKET/a2/matrix.parquet,--zones,s3://$BUCKET/a2/raw/zones.parquet,--out,s3://$BUCKET/a2/stage2-2n,--platform,emr,--fit-rounds,50]" \
  --query 'StepIds[0]' --output text)
save STEP_ID "$STEP_ID"
Watch it, and note when it first reports COMPLETED.
aws emr describe-step --cluster-id $CLUSTER_ID --step-id $STEP_ID --region ca-central-1 \
  --query 'Step.Status.{State:State,Start:Timeline.StartDateTime,End:Timeline.EndDateTime}'
The script prints its metrics blocks on stdout, which EMR archives under your --log-uri a few minutes after the step ends. Pull it down and unzip it.
aws s3 cp s3://$BUCKET/a2/emr-logs/$CLUSTER_ID/steps/$STEP_ID/stdout.gz - --region ca-central-1 \
  | gunzip > stage2-2n.log
grep -c '===A2-METRICS' stage2-2n.log      # 2: one for A_aggregate, one for B_fit

Note📋 Commands: Resize and re-run





Grow the cluster in place rather than launching a second one. Find the CORE group first.
aws emr describe-cluster --cluster-id $CLUSTER_ID --region ca-central-1 \
  --query "Cluster.InstanceGroups[?InstanceGroupType=='CORE'].{Id:Id,Type:InstanceType,Running:RunningInstanceCount,State:Status.State}"
IG_ID=$(aws emr describe-cluster --cluster-id $CLUSTER_ID --region ca-central-1 \
  --query "Cluster.InstanceGroups[?InstanceGroupType=='CORE'].Id | [0]" --output text)
save IG_ID "$IG_ID"
aws emr modify-instance-groups --region ca-central-1 \
  --instance-groups InstanceGroupId=$IG_ID,InstanceCount=4
Re-run the same describe-cluster call until Running reads 4 and the group’s state is RUNNING. Submitting before then measures a 3-node cluster and quietly ruins the comparison.
Then wait about two more minutes before you submit. The instance group reports the new nodes as running some way before Spark has an executor on each of them, and a step that starts early runs part of phase A on half the cluster you are paying for.
Then submit the identical step with a new output prefix. save replaces the step id with the new one.
STEP_ID=$(aws emr add-steps --cluster-id $CLUSTER_ID --region ca-central-1 \
  --steps "Type=Spark,Name=a2-stage2-4n,ActionOnFailure=CONTINUE,Args=[--deploy-mode,client,s3://$BUCKET/a2/stages/stage2_spark.py,--trips,s3://$BUCKET/a2/matrix.parquet,--zones,s3://$BUCKET/a2/raw/zones.parquet,--out,s3://$BUCKET/a2/stage2-4n,--platform,emr,--fit-rounds,50]" \
  --query 'StepIds[0]' --output text)
save STEP_ID "$STEP_ID"
Watch it with the same describe-step call as the 2-node run, which now reads the new step id, until it reports COMPLETED. Then pull its log, which arrives a few minutes after the step ends.
aws s3 cp s3://$BUCKET/a2/emr-logs/$CLUSTER_ID/steps/$STEP_ID/stdout.gz - --region ca-central-1 \
  | gunzip > stage2-4n.log
grep -c '===A2-METRICS' stage2-4n.log      # 2
Before you parse it, check that the run had all four nodes. The step’s driver log prints one Registered executor line per executor, and all four have to arrive before the first stage is submitted. Fewer than four means the wait was too short and the 4-node run is not comparable to the 2-node one: submit the step again. That log is stderr.gz, beside the stdout.gz you just pulled.
aws s3 cp s3://$BUCKET/a2/emr-logs/$CLUSTER_ID/steps/$STEP_ID/stderr.gz - --region ca-central-1 \
  | gunzip | grep -c 'Registered executor'      # 4
python3 stages/parse_run_log.py stage2-4n.log --resource-id $CLUSTER_ID --nodes 4

A2 DRAFT: Spark and Glue: Exploring performance and cost
text:
3.2 Measure
rubric={correctness:5}
Submit the job (see 📋 below). The job-run page reports startup and execution separately, so keep them in separate columns. Parse both blocks into 3_glue rows with nodes set to your worker count, and cost from the Glue rate for ca-central-1.







Note📋 Commands: Stage 3 on Glue





The script in S3 is the one EMR just ran, byte for byte. Only the submission changes.
Glue needs a role it can assume itself. A fresh account has none (the 2026-08 pilot’s did not). Create it once, with the same create-then-attach move as the instance role:
aws iam create-role --role-name $CWL-a2-glue-role \
  --assume-role-policy-document '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"glue.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole"}]}'
aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name $CWL-a2-glue-role \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSGlueServiceRole
aws iam put-role-policy --role-name $CWL-a2-glue-role --policy-name a2-s3 \
  --policy-document file://$HOME/a2-s3-policy.json
Create the job with 3 G.1X workers. The assignment says why that is the number.
aws glue create-job --region ca-central-1 \
  --name $CWL-a2-stage3 \
  --role $CWL-a2-glue-role \
  --glue-version 6.0 \
  --worker-type G.1X --number-of-workers 3 \
  --command Name=glueetl,ScriptLocation=s3://$BUCKET/a2/stages/stage2_spark.py,PythonVersion=3 \
  --no-job-run-queuing-enabled \
  --default-arguments '{"--conf":"spark.ui.enabled=true","--enable-auto-scaling":"false"}'
Those are the only two default arguments the job takes. --conf is one key holding one string, so a second Spark setting joins that same value ("spark.ui.enabled=true --conf spark.other=x") rather than arriving as a second key, which would overwrite the first.
--enable-auto-scaling stays "false". With autoscaling on, the worker count moves during the run and stops being the constant this whole comparison rests on. spark.ui.enabled=true keeps the driver’s REST endpoint alive, which is where the script reads its metrics from.
cat > stage3-args.json <<EOF
{"--trips":"s3://$BUCKET/a2/matrix.parquet","--zones":"s3://$BUCKET/a2/raw/zones.parquet","--out":"s3://$BUCKET/a2/stage3","--platform":"glue","--fit-rounds":"50"}
EOF
JOB_RUN_ID=$(aws glue start-job-run --region ca-central-1 \
  --job-name $CWL-a2-stage3 \
  --arguments file://stage3-args.json \
  --query 'JobRunId' --output text)
save JOB_RUN_ID "$JOB_RUN_ID"
The script’s own flags travel as Glue job arguments, which is why they keep their -- prefixes here. Glue injects arguments of its own, --JOB_NAME among them, and the script ignores anything it does not recognise.
A run that reports FAILED within seconds, with an error saying the role “should be given assume role permissions for Glue Service”, started before the new role had spread through IAM, which takes up to a minute after create-role. Nothing is wrong with the role: wait a minute and start the run again.
Starting a second run the moment the first reports SUCCEEDED gets you ConcurrentRunsExceededException. The state flips before the run’s slot is released, and this job is created with queuing off, so the new run is rejected rather than held. Wait about a minute and start it again.
Read the timings off the run record.
aws glue get-job-run --job-name $CWL-a2-stage3 --run-id $JOB_RUN_ID --region ca-central-1 \
  --query 'JobRun.{State:JobRunState,Started:StartedOn,Completed:CompletedOn,Execution:ExecutionTime,DPUSeconds:DPUSeconds}'
startup_s is elapsed time minus ExecutionTime: take Completed minus Started in seconds and subtract the execution seconds. The console prints the same figure as the run’s start-up time. Save it, with your number in place of 42:
save STARTUP_S 42
For DPU-seconds, use the DPUSeconds field when it is populated, otherwise 3 workers times ExecutionTime, since G.1X bills 1 DPU per worker.
The driver’s stdout goes to the CloudWatch log group /aws-glue/jobs/output, in a stream named for the run id exactly, with nothing on the end. That one stream is the driver’s, and it holds both metrics blocks. The executor streams live in /aws-glue/jobs/error under names like your run id followed by _g-<hash>, and hold no metrics blocks.
aws logs get-log-events --region ca-central-1 \
  --log-group-name /aws-glue/jobs/output --log-stream-name $JOB_RUN_ID \
  --start-from-head --output text --query 'events[*].message' \
  | tr '\t' '\n' > stage3.log
grep -c '===A2-METRICS' stage3.log         # 2
The tr puts one log message per line, which the parser needs. If the count comes back under 2, the stream is paginated: open the same log group from the job-run page in the console and copy the output from there. Then parse, with the startup seconds you just computed.
python3 stages/parse_run_log.py stage3.log --resource-id $JOB_RUN_ID --nodes 3 --startup-s $STARTUP_S

Tip📐 Prediction 4, how many runs before EMR costs less than Glue?



(launch + N × work) × cluster_rate = N × (startup + work) × dpu_rate

Launch. Your measured EMR launch_s, the gap from the create call to WAITING. Write it in hours.
Work. The job’s own wall time, phase A plus phase B, from your 2-node EMR run. Write it in hours.
Cluster rate. The hourly rate for a 1-primary, 2-core m7g.xlarge cluster, from the price sheet. The primary node is billed too, so write the rate for all three nodes.
Startup. Your measured Glue startup_s, in hours.
DPU rate. The Glue per-DPU-hour rate for ca-central-1, times your DPU count. A DPU, or Data Processing Unit, is the unit Glue bills in, and G.1X bills 1 DPU per worker, so your 3 workers are 3 DPU for as long as the run lasts. Write the rate and the count you used.

Put every time in hours before you substitute. The left side prices one launch amortised over N runs done back to back. Solve for N, and show the rearrangement as well as the answer.
